extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and instructors studying ordinary differential equations
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, hypotheses, and constructive methods for existence, uniqueness, continuous/smooth dependence on initial data and parameters, and solution structure of linear systems and constant-coefficient ODEs. Includes techniques (Picard iteration, Wronskian, variation of parameters) and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and boundedness of F for existence
rubrics_metrics.description: F : D → R^n (or C^n) continuous and bounded on a compact rectangle R around (t0,y0) ensures existence of a solution of the integral/ODE on a (possibly small) time interval about t0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a rectangle R (in t and y) contained in D and an upper bound M for |F| on R; pick a0 depending on M so that the Picard iterates remain in R. Theorem 4.1 (existence) is proved constructively by successive approximations y_{n+1}(t)=y0 + ∫_{t0}^t F(s,y_n(s)) ds and uniform convergence via the Weierstrass M-test. The text shows explicit bounds (involving M, k, a0) controlling the iterates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lipschitz condition in y-variable (criterion for uniqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: F(t,y) satisfies a Lipschitz condition in the y variable on D: |F(t,y1) - F(t,y2)| ≤ k |y1 - y2| for (t,y1),(t,y2) in D, for some constant k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Lipschitz hypothesis is used to prove uniqueness (Theorem 4.2) and to get contraction-like estimates on differences of successive approximations. The text gives inductive estimates and bounds (involving k and M) that show differences go to zero; Gronwall-type/induction arguments yield uniqueness on an interval |t-t0|<a0. It is standard to assume k>0 and to restrict to a small time interval if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picard iteration and uniform convergence criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct sequence y0,y1,... by y_{n+1}(t)=y0+∫_{t0}^t F(s,y_n(s)) ds; under boundedness and Lipschitz hypotheses the sequence converges uniformly to a continuous solution y(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit estimates |y_{n+1}-y_n| ≤ M k^n (a0)^n / n! (or similar) independent of (t,t0,y0) to apply the Weierstrass M-test. The uniform limit is continuous and satisfies the integral equation; this is the constructive proof of existence. The text carries out base case and inductive step with detailed factorial estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness theorem for initial-value problems
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is continuous on D and satisfies a Lipschitz condition in y, then for given (t0,y0) there exists at most one solution y(t) on the interval |t-t0|<a00 satisfying y(t0)=y0 (Theorem 4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof compares two solutions y and z, estimates |y(t)-z(t)| by integrating the Lipschitz difference and iterating to produce bounds tending to zero. The text shows a full inductive estimate and concludes equality for all t in the interval. This is the standard uniqueness (Gronwall/iteration) argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous dependence of solution on initial data and parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Under continuity of F and a Lipschitz condition in y, the unique solution y(t,t0,y0) depends continuously on (t,t0,y0) on an appropriate open set U (Theorem 4.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction uses the same Picard iterates defined for each (t0,y0) and shows uniform convergence of yn(t,t0,y0) to y(t,t0,y0) on U via bounds independent of (t0,y0). The text gives the rectangle/compact-set method, chooses δ-η for uniform continuity, and proves continuity by estimating differences of iterates and using uniform M-test bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth dependence if F is smooth
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is smooth on D then the solution map (t,t0,y0) ↦ y(t,t0,y0) is smooth on the open set U where solutions exist (Theorem 4.3, proof of smoothness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show each Picard iterate yn(t,t0,y0) is smooth by induction using the chain rule and Fundamental Theorem of Calculus; estimate derivatives to get uniform convergence of iterated partial derivatives, hence smoothness of the limit. Parameters can be treated by adjoining them as extra variables (see concluding remark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter incorporation via additional variables
rubrics_metrics.description: To study dependence on parameters π1,...,πk in F(t,y,π), introduce additional variables z_j with z'_j = 0 and initial z_j(t0)=π_j, reducing parameter-dependence questions to the standard initial-value problem framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trick reduces smooth/continuous parameter dependence to the case covered by Theorem 4.3: treat parameters as extra constant coordinates and apply existence/uniqueness/smoothness results to the enlarged system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness of integral curves for smooth vector fields
rubrics_metrics.description: If X : U → R^n is a smooth vector field on an open U and p∈U, then there exists ε>0 and an integral curve c:(-ε,ε)→U with c'(t)=X(c(t)) and c(0)=p; any two integral curves coincide on overlaps (Proposition 4.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an application of the ODE existence/uniqueness theorems to the autonomous system c' = X(c). Smoothness of X gives smoothness of c by Theorem 4.3; uniqueness follows from Theorem 4.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smooth family of integral curves for parameterized vector fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Given smooth vector fields X^{(1)},...,X^{(m)} and parameters ρ in a neighborhood V of 0, define X_ρ = Σ ρ_j X^{(j)}: then there exist integral curves c(t,ρ) smooth in (t,ρ), unique in a small time interval, and if m ≥ n and the vectors X^{(1)}(p),...,X^{(n)}(p) are linearly independent then the Jacobian ∂c(δ,ρ)/∂ρ at ρ=0 is nonsingular for small δ>0 (Proposition 4.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the parameterized ODE as depending smoothly on parameters and apply Theorem 4.3. The nonsingularity conclusion follows by differentiating with respect to parameters and evaluating at ρ=0; use the Inverse Function Theorem to obtain local coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of higher-order scalar ODE to first-order system
rubrics_metrics.description: A single nth-order linear ODE can be converted to a first-order linear system y' = A(t)y + Q(t) by setting y = (y, y',...,y^{(n-1)})^T; the companion matrix A(t) has continuous entries when coefficients are continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conversion allows application of existence/uniqueness theory for first-order systems and clarifies that initial values for y and its derivatives up to order n-1 determine the unique solution. The companion matrix form is explicitly given in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic Lipschitz property for linear systems with continuous coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For a linear system y' = A(t)y + Q(t) with A(t),Q(t) continuous, the right-hand side satisfies a Lipschitz condition in y on compact subintervals (since ||A(t)(y1-y2)|| ≤ ||A(t)||·||y1-y2||).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus existence and uniqueness follow directly for linear systems; any local solution extends uniquely and depends continuously on initial data. Use a bound on ||A(t)|| on the compact set to obtain the Lipschitz constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension and dimension properties of homogeneous linear systems
rubrics_metrics.description: For y' = A(t)y with A(t) continuous on (a,b): (a) any solution on a subinterval extends to a solution on whole (a,b); (b) the vector space of solutions on any subinterval has dimension exactly n; (c) solutions v1,...,vr are linearly independent iff their column vectors at any t0 are linearly independent (Theorem 4.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses existence/uniqueness to extend local bases and uniqueness to relate linear dependence of functions to linear dependence of their initial values. To show extension, construct maximal solution and extend by matching to local bases near endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wronskian criterion for linear independence of solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If v1,...,vn are solutions of an n×n homogeneous linear system and W(t) is the matrix with columns vj(t), then v1,...,vn are linearly independent iff det W(t) is nowhere 0 (equivalently det W is nonzero at some point) (Proposition 4.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since W'(t)=A(t)W(t), invertibility/nonvanishing determinant at one point implies invertibility on the interval; examples: for y''+y=0 the fundamental solutions cos t and sin t give W(t) with determinant 1. Use evaluation at a single t0 to test independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: General solution structure for inhomogeneous linear systems
rubrics_metrics.description: For y' = A(t)y + Q(t) with continuous A,Q, any particular solution y* plus any solution h of the homogeneous system gives a general solution y = y* + h. Also any local solution extends to the whole domain (Proposition 4.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difference of two particular solutions solves the homogeneous system. Existence/uniqueness and extension results ensure one can freely add homogeneous solutions to a particular one to obtain all solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of parameters for first-order linear systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Given linearly independent fundamental solutions v1,...,vn with Wronskian W(t), a particular solution of y' = A(t)y + Q(t) is y*(t) = W(t) u(t) where u'(t) solves W(t) u'(t) = Q(t), so y*(t) = W(t) ∫^t W(s)^{-1} Q(s) ds (Theorem 4.9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires W(t) invertible (i.e., fundamental solutions independent) and A,Q continuous so W^{-1}Q is continuous and integrable. The text emphasizes existence of fundamental solutions (Theorem 4.6) and gives the explicit integral formula for u.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant-coefficient homogeneous ODE: characteristic polynomial and solution basis
rubrics_metrics.description: For constant-coefficient linear ODE L(y)=0 with characteristic polynomial P(r)=∏ (r - r_j)^{m_j}, the functions e^{r_j t}, t e^{r_j t}, ..., t^{m_j-1} e^{r_j t} (for each distinct root r_j of multiplicity m_j) form a basis of solutions on any interval (Proposition 4.12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show these functions satisfy the differential operator factors (Lemma 4.10), prove linear independence (Lemma 4.11) by reducing to polynomial-coefficient relations, and count n linearly independent solutions to get a basis. Example: repeated roots produce polynomial multiples of exponentials; distinct complex roots handled similarly (complex-valued solutions).
